title: Ethnographic Theorizing in Human Resource Management: From Theory‐as‐Design to Theory‐in‐Use
abstract: ABSTRACT Research on human resource management (HRM) has generated influential frameworks for explaining the relationships between HR practices and organizational outcomes. Existing accounts offer less insight into how the frameworks informing those practices acquire meaning, authority, and practical traction in organizational settings. We conceptualize this as a gap between theory‐as‐design and theory‐in‐use and develop ethnographic theorizing as a mode of examining the use‐life of selected design‐oriented HRM frameworks. Our contribution is twofold. First, we specify how sustained immersion, temporal depth, embodied co‐presence, and relational obligation enable researchers to follow frameworks as they are enacted and negotiated. Second, we develop three recursively related analytic moves for theory development— Complement, Complicate, and Reframe —through which ethnographic evidence can elaborate, qualify, or revise existing theoretical accounts. We demonstrate this approach through two ethnographic studies of HR analytics in different organizations. The comparison shows how legitimacy work, identity negotiation, and meaning‐making shaped the enactment of data‐driven HRM in these settings. The paper thus offers a structured approach for studying how established HRM frameworks operate in use and for assessing when situated evidence warrants changes to their constructs, relationships, or boundary conditions. In addition, we discuss implications for HRM theory, research design, and practice.

title: Combining management control practices for organizational learning: A situational strength perspective
abstract: Organizational learning (OL) is a critical organizational capability. Yet designing management control (MC) that effectively supports OL is challenging, as learning outcomes are often intangible and unfold over extended time horizons. Employing situational strength theory, we examine combinations of MC practices that affect OL contingent on environmental uncertainty. Drawing on a survey of 210 senior business unit controllers, we use fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) to identify multiple combinations of MC practices that achieve high OL in different uncertainty contexts. In a subsequent step, we examine whether the situational strength of certain combinations of MC practices is associated with OL. Results show that in a low-uncertainty environment, the combined use of diverse performance measures and social controls, as well as performance pay and a mechanistic administrative structure, have a synergetic effect on OL. In a high-uncertainty context, the combined use of measure diversity and deliberate formal strategic planning is beneficial for achieving OL. Our results suggest that the effectiveness of MC practices for OL depends on aligning MC practices with the internal as well as the external context.

title: EXPRESS: Evaluating the Impacts of Bundling on a Firm’s Product Demand and Operational Decisions
abstract: Firms use bundles to influence customer demand, but supplying those bundles often requires operational capacity that is shared across the portfolio. Changing the price, composition, or availability of one bundle can therefore trigger two reallocations: customers reallocate expenditure across bundles, and the firm reallocates operational capacity across the demand those bundles generate. We develop a data-driven framework that links these two decisions. Heterogeneous consumers choose discrete bundle quantities subject to a common budget, while the firm jointly chooses bundle prices and quantities subject to bundle-specific and shared-resource requirements. We estimate the demand and supply models from observed discrete decisions using Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo, retaining the integer structure in estimation and counterfactual analysis. We apply the framework to three empirical settings: public bike sharing, online retail, and theme-park services. The empirical analyses reveal several consequences of evaluating bundles as part of a portfolio. Customer value and profit contribution need not be aligned: a bundle that creates substantial customer value can make little or no incremental contribution to optimized profit, and removing some bundles can increase profit after the remaining portfolio is re-optimized. Price responses differ across bundles because discrete purchases adjust at different thresholds. A bundle's response to tighter shared-resource requirements depends on how its resource use changes the allocation of operational capacity elsewhere in the portfolio, rather than on its characteristics alone. Finally, deeper discounts need not generate larger incremental profit contributions; in the theme-park application, an intermediate discount can outperform both deeper and shallower discounts after the portfolio is re-optimized. Bundle design is a portfolio problem: a bundle's contribution depends not only on the demand it generates, but also on the customer and operational adjustments it induces elsewhere in the portfolio.

title: Who Gains from creative destruction? Evidence from high-quality entrepreneurship in the United States
abstract: The question of who gains from high-quality entrepreneurship is crucial to understanding whether investments in innovative startup firms produce socially beneficial outcomes. Although entrepreneurship is widely viewed as a central driver of economic growth, recent research has raised concerns that it may also exacerbate inequality and other undesirable social outcomes. We bring new evidence to this debate by analyzing the impact of entrepreneurship on a variety of local economic outcomes, including income inequality, average incomes, and income mobility, using IRS and U.S. Census Bureau microdata. We find that entrepreneurship indeed increases income inequality, although this effect fades in the years after firm founding. While entrepreneurship produces statistically significant income gains across the distribution, the economic magnitude of these effects varies dramatically, with benefits concentrated among top earners. We also find that entrepreneurship can serve as a mobility tool for less well-off individuals, increasing their probability of rising to the top of the income distribution. These income and mobility gains, however, are uneven across demographic groups.

title: A platform for change? Core component innovations, complementor adaptation, and multihoming in platform‐based ecosystems
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Digital platforms coordinate complementor innovations through interfaces into their core components. However, when interfaces themselves evolve alongside core component innovations, complementors may exhibit behaviors that are not entirely predictable. Using granular data from Apple's five major iOS releases, we abductively examine App developers’ responses following Apple's core component innovations. We document that, in post‐release periods, complementors simultaneously increase co‐innovation on iOS while being more likely to multihome by diversifying to the competing platform. These choices are further explained by whether architectural changes reflect cross‐platform standardization or platform‐specific differentiation. Standardization spurs both complementor co‐innovation and multihoming, while differentiation reduces diversification tendencies. The patterns that we document reveal an important tension: governing through interfaces enables platforms’ scalability but constrains their ability to control complementors as platforms evolve. Managerial Summary Digital platforms like Apple coordinate large scale innovation through standardized interfaces, but those interfaces must evolve as platforms compete, and the direction of that evolution has consequences managers should attend to. Analyzing Apple's five major iOS releases, we find that architectural changes are associated with increased co‐innovation but also a higher likelihood that developers diversify to a competing platform. This pattern is particularly pronounced when updates bring iOS closer to Android, suggesting that architectural convergence may lower the barriers to cross‐platform expansion for developers. Importantly, this behavior is strongest among highest‐value developers. Platform managers should therefore treat architectural evolution not merely as a technical decision, but as a strategic one with direct implications for ecosystem loyalty, competitive differentiation, and the retention of valuable ecosystem partners.

title: Competition and Diversity in Generative AI
abstract: Recent evidence, both in the laboratory and in the wild, suggests that the use of generative artificial intelligence reduces the diversity of content produced. As generative AI penetrates more markets and reaches widespread adoption, should we still expect to see content homogenization? Our work begins with a simple observation: content producers do not act in isolation. Instead, they compete with one another (e.g., for customers or attention). We explore the impact competition has on both content diversity and overall social welfare when producers use generative AI. Through a formal game-theoretic model, we show that competitive markets select for diverse AI models, mitigating monoculture. We further show that a generative AI model that performs well in isolation (i.e., according to a benchmark) may fail to provide value in a competitive market. Our results highlight the importance of evaluating generative AI models across the breadth of their output distributions, particularly when they will be deployed in competitive environments. We validate our theoretical results with a series of experiments involving generative text and image models. Overall, our results suggest that homogenization due to generative AI is unlikely to persist under strong competition. This paper was accepted by Itai Ashlagi, market design, platform, and demand analytics. title: The Buy-in Effect: When Increasing Initial Effort Encourages Follow-Through
abstract: Behavioral interventions often focus on reducing friction to encourage behavior change. In contrast, we provide evidence that adding initial friction to a sign-up process can increase follow-through behavior. In a field experiment with a state department of transportation ([Formula: see text]), we test whether adding modest friction during sign-up for a carpool platform increases usage. Although a more effortful sign-up process leads to 25% fewer sign-ups, overall usage increases. Importantly, these results were only partly explained by selection: Using an intent-to-treat analysis, participants with a more effortful sign-up process took 1.6 times more carpool trips per week over four months, leading to more overall trips despite fewer users. In a second experiment with online task work, participants with more effortful sign-up were 37% more likely to return the next day and completed more work overall. These results suggest that adding friction may be an overlooked strategy when follow-through, rather than initial uptake, is the primary goal. This paper was accepted by George Wu, behavioral economics and decision analysis. title: Simulating competitive collocation strategies with deep reinforcement learning
abstract: Abstract This paper introduces a simulation model based on deep reinforcement learning to study competitive collocation strategies of two internationalizing firms. Drawing on the strategic interaction and competitive collocation literature in IB, we explore the factors determining the performance-optimizing degree of collocation in market-seeking internationalization for a duopoly in product markets. Our simulation suggests that a high degree of collocation between the two firms is optimal in many circumstances. Whereas mid-to-high levels of collocation are driven by low competitive intensity, low entry barriers, low home-market size, and high market-size variation, complete collocation emerges under high competitive intensity, low first-mover advantage, and smaller home-market size. High entry barriers, combined with low variation in market size and strong liabilities of foreignness, drive the opposite case of complete mutual avoidance. A key takeaway from the simulation is a focus on the competing firm in global expansion: in many cases, it becomes key to limit the rival’s growth options and to enter key markets before access becomes more restricted. We discuss the possibilities of using computer-simulation-based approaches to theorizing on internationalization.

title: CEO Ideologically (In)Congruent Activism and Investor Reactions: An Attribution of CEO Intentions Perspective
abstract: Abstract The phenomenon of chief executive officers (CEOs) taking activism stances on contested sociopolitical issues is increasing, yet it remains unclear how observing investors discern CEO intentions behind activism engagements, thereby shaping their judgments and subsequent reactions. By relaxing the assumption that CEO activism is an unabashed expression of personal beliefs, we propose the concept of CEO ideologically (in)congruent activism and develop a framework wherein investors may attribute CEO intentions underlying incongruent (versus congruent) activism engagements as more organization‐driven (versus self‐driven) interest pursuits, thereby leading to more positive investor evaluations and reactions. Furthermore, we argue that the positive effect of CEO ideologically incongruent activism on investor reactions will be amplified when the CEO owns a higher level of stock ownership but weakened when the firm receives a greater corporate social responsibility (CSR) rating. We corroborate our propositions using a sample of CEO activism events for S&P 500 firms from 2012 to 2021. Our findings demonstrate the heterogeneity and critical influence of CEO intentions behind activism engagements and shed light on how investors integrate multi‐informational cues when evaluating and reacting to managerial incongruent behaviours.

title: Measuring Organizational Constructs in Large-Scale Text: An interpretive framework combining topic modeling and BERT
abstract: Measuring organizational constructs in large-scale unstructured text requires methods that preserve interpretive depth while enabling systematic, per-document classification. Structural Topic Modeling (STM) supports interpretive depth by surfacing patterns that inform construct operationalization, but its topic proportions are not designed as standalone per-document construct measures; transformer-based models such as BERT can scale measurement but require construct operationalization grounded in interpretive work. We address this challenge through a two-stage framework in which STM and BERT play structurally distinct roles. Coding schemes are developed through qualitative interpretation and STM analysis; BERT is then fine-tuned to apply these schemes across documents. We formalize two research approaches—construct-guided and pattern-discovery—that provide principled paths from different theoretical starting points toward a shared methodological endpoint: validated, auditable per-document construct measures. We illustrate the framework using more than 20,000 employee reviews. The framework supports iterative construct validation, using computational diagnostics to guide interpretive refinement and producing document-level measures suitable for theory-informed organizational analysis.

Measuring Measurement Error
abstract: Abstract We collect 2,848 instrumental variable (IV) regressions from 391 papers published in top economics and finance journals and show that estimated IV coefficients are often much larger than their OLS counterparts, even when theory suggests they should be smaller. We derive meta-regression estimators that distinguish measurement error bias from omitted variable bias and simultaneity bias; applying our estimators to a set of 1,040 comparable regressions from 139 papers, we find that measurement error shrinks reported coefficients by about two to four times. Measurement error remains quantitatively important even after accounting for weak instruments, publication bias, instrument invalidity, and heterogeneous treatment effects. Our results suggest that measurement error is a severe, pervasive, and understated source of bias in economics and finance.

title: A Preconditioned Augmented Lagrangian Method for Solving Semidefinite Programming Problems
abstract: In this work, we propose a preconditioned augmented Lagrangian method (ALM) for solving semidefinite programming (SDP) problems. The preconditioner is implemented via a weighted penalty function in the ALM subproblem, with the weight matrix derived from the projection operator onto the tangent space of the feasible region. This simple yet effective modification significantly accelerates ALM, particularly for ill-conditioned SDPs. By combining the preconditioned ALM with our previously developed feasible method, SDPF, we develop SDPF+, an SDP solver capable of handling convex problems with possibly nonlinear objective functions. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate the efficiency and robustness of SDPF+, showing that it can generally outperform other solvers on large-scale SDPs whose optimal solutions exhibit low-rank structure. title: Revenue Maximization for Seaport Terminal Operations Considering Multimodal Cargo Flows
abstract: We study the optimal pricing problem for operations at a seaport terminal within a multimodal transport network, where the terminal operator sets differentiated prices for processing cargoes arriving via and transferred to various modes of transport. The problem incorporates two critical features: (i) the influence of port congestion on cargo suppliers’ terminal selection and (ii) the hierarchical choice structure that predicts how cargo suppliers select transport modes and routes for their cargoes. To capture these features, we formulate the problem as a nonconvex, nonlinear program involving a nested logit choice model and an equilibrium constraint reflecting the congestion effect, which is challenging to solve or analyze. To address this difficulty, we apply a change of variables to reformulate the price-based model as a flow-based model, where cargo flows, rather than prices, are the decision variables, thereby making the model more amenable to analysis. By exploiting the structure of the flow-based model, we derive an optimality equation whose dimension scales only with the number of origin-destination (O/D) pairs, which effectively reduces the computational complexity by avoiding directly handling the numerous variables associated with transport routes. This approach not only applies to seaport revenue management problems that often involve multiple transport modes and a substantial number of routes, but also contributes a structure-exploiting method for addressing a broader class of nonlinear programs involving equilibrium constraints and customer choice models. We show that, for each O/D pair, the optimal mode-dependent prices decompose into a component common across modes plus a mode-specific adjustment. We also establish analytical bounds on the revenue loss induced by misspecifying cargo suppliers’ choice structure. We evaluate the performance of the algorithm by comparing it with several widely used benchmark methods through numerical analysis. Our findings indicate that our algorithm outperforms the benchmark methods in both revenue maximization and runtime. Moreover, we find that accurately modeling the choice structure has a larger impact on revenue than explicitly modeling congestion. title: A Novel and Efficient Formulation and Solution Approach for the Region Coverage Problem with Identical Circles
abstract: The problem of covering a two-dimensional region with identical circles of minimal radius (CRICMR) is a classic optimization problem with many relevant real-world applications. However, due to the nonconvexity and the multiply-connected nature of the region to be covered, designing an efficient formulation and solution approach for the problem is very challenging. In this study, we first propose a unified optimization model for two classic variants of the problem (i.e., the CRICMR problems with and without center placement constraints), and then present an effective heuristic algorithm for solving both variants. The proposed model is based on the clipped Voronoi diagram and converts the intractable region coverage problem into the much easier vertex covering problem with respect to the clipped Voronoi polygons. The proposed algorithm incorporates several key components: a two-phase monotonic basin-hopping method; a subregion-based local optimization method; two perturbation operators, and a radius adjustment method for the covering circles. Computational experiments on popular benchmark instances demonstrate the efficiency of our approach, which significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods by improving the current best-known solutions for nearly all benchmark instances. title: Dialysis Clinic Patient Flow and Work Design
abstract: Problem Definition: For 433,000 patients in the United States with advanced kidney failure, hemodialysis is a life-sustaining treatment. Approximately 7,600 outpatient dialysis clinics serve these patients, whose treatments cost over $25 billion annually. Each treatment involves a pre-treatment “put-on” task and a post-treatment “take-off” task performed by patient care technicians (PCTs). These frontline workers face intense, overlapping demands that can compromise patient safety and contribute to PCT burnout. We study how to jointly schedule PCTs and patients to reduce makespan and increase labor efficiency in dialysis clinic operations through better patient flow. Methodology/Results: We first analyze the prevailing “push” approach, which starts put-ons as soon as a technician and station are free. We then propose two alternatives: an “interlaced” scheme that staggers put-ons and take-offs to reduce idle time, and a “tandem” scheme that pairs two PCTs — one specializing in put-ons and the other in take-offs — across twice as many stations. We derive closed-form expressions for each approach’s makespan under constant treatment durations and show that interlaced schedules achieve the shortest completion time, whereas tandem configurations can reduce labor per patient. We also incorporate heterogeneous treatment durations and stochastic task times and arrivals to show numerically that our insights are robust. Managerial Implications: In contrast to the push-focused approach, these insights direct facility administrators’ attention to the primary driver of labor efficiency: minimizing the time that stations sit unoccupied between successive patients. Due to the inefficiencies of the push approach for a single pod, transitioning to an interlaced or tandem system while increasing the standard time allotted for tasks can alleviate workplace stress and promote patient safety without increasing labor costs. Specifically, dialysis clinic managers could move from the common 15/15-minute put-on/take-off scheduling standard to a 25/20-minute standard, thereby allotting PCTs 50% more time to complete tasks. Methodology/Results: We first analyze the prevailing “push” approach, which starts put-on tasks for treatment as soon as a station is free. We then propose two alternatives: an “interlaced” scheme that staggers put-ons and take-offs to reduce idle time, and a “tandem” scheme that pairs two PCTs — one specializing in put-ons, the other in take-offs — across twice as many stations. Under standard conditions, we derive closed-form expressions for each approach’s completion time and show that interlacing finishes earliest with homogeneous treatment durations, while tandem configurations can lower labor per patient. We also incorporate heterogeneous treatment durations to show numerically that our insights are robust. Managerial Implications: In contrast to the push-focused approach, these insights direct facility administrators’ attention to what is most important for labor efficiency: minimizing the time that a station is unoccupied between successive patients. Due to the inefficiencies associated with the push approach, transitioning to an interlaced or tandem system with increased standard task times can alleviate workplace stress and promote patient safety without increasing labor costs. Specifically, dialysis clinic managers could move from the common 15/15-minute put-on/take-off scheduling standard to a 25/20-minute standard, thereby allotting PCTs 50% more time to complete tasks.

title: Enhancing Safety Signaling: Integrating Clinical Trials and Post-Marketing Adverse Event Reports
abstract: Problem definition: Adverse drug reactions (ADRs) cause numerous emergency room visits and thousands of deaths annually in the U.S. Although regulators like the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) aim to detect safety issues during clinical trials, these trials are often too small, short, or restrictive to capture rare or delayed ADRs. Consequently, regulators rely on spontaneous adverse event reporting systems (eg, FAERS) to identify potential safety issues—termed safety signals—by detecting side effects that occur disproportionately among patients taking a particular drug. However, these observational data are subject to selection and reporting biases, which can lead to false signals or missed risks. Methodology/results: We propose a Bayesian framework to enhance the hypothesis generation step in safety signaling, offering two methodological advances over standard approaches that rely solely on observational data. First, it integrates pre-approval clinical trial and post-approval observational data. Second, it uses information from common ADRs to estimate and correct bias in rare ADRs. We assess the approach using an analytical model and a large-scale numerical study with real clinical trial and FAERS data. Incorporating clinical trial data substantially reduces signaling costs, and using a common ADR for debiasing yields further gains. This refinement improves decisions for about 1% of ADRs, translating to expected cost savings of 1.5–2.3% (approx. $32–159 million), with performance robust to moderate parameter misspecification. Managerial implications: By using existing regulatory data, our approach supports a more efficient and timely hypothesis generation process in post-approval surveillance.

title: Big Data Development and Corporate Environmental Strategy: Evidence from Green Innovation Engagement
Innovation adoption across regions: psychological openness and the early diffusion of digital platforms
abstract: Early regional adoption is crucial for platform-enabled innovations because their viability depends on enough people within a region adopting them to generate network effects. Existing research on regional innovation diffusion explains early adoption largely through demographic, economic, infrastructural, or institutional conditions, paying limited attention to regional population psychology. We conceptualize regional psychological openness as an invisible social infrastructure that is relevant for understanding early platform adoption. To test this idea, we introduce a newly curated dataset that allows us to trace the initial development of three major platform innovations (i.e., accommodation sharing platforms, ride-sharing platforms, social media platforms) across hundreds of U.S. metropolitan regions. Across all three platform types, regions differ markedly in early adoption. We link these adoption data to large-scale geo-referenced personality information from millions of U.S. residents ( N = 3,234,899). Results show that regional psychological openness consistently predicts earlier uptake even after accounting for demographic, socio-economic, social, infrastructural, geographical, and other psychological characteristics. In sum, the study advances a behavioral perspective on regional innovation adoption by integrating population psychology into explanations of platform diffusion.

title: External collaboration and local knowledge divergence in regional knowledge spaces
abstract: This study investigates the association between regional collaboration structures and the semantic position of locally produced scientific knowledge. Drawing on the Regional Innovation Systems framework, it distinguishes between intra-regional and inter-regional collaboration as complementary dimensions of scientific knowledge production. Using over nine million Web of Science publications from European regions between 1998 and 2021, this study employs semantic text embeddings to measure local knowledge divergence, defined as the semantic distance between each publication and the established regional knowledge base. Within the same region–field–period, externally collaborated publication groups exhibit slightly higher average local knowledge divergence than internally collaborated groups. However, the estimated difference is substantively negligible and varies across periods. The principal pooled-sample finding is an inverted U-shaped association between external collaboration share and regional local knowledge divergence, with the fitted curve reaching its maximum at an external collaboration share of approximately 45%. The realised magnitude of this association is modest, and heterogeneity analyses show that it is most pronounced in life sciences and biomedicine and after 2010. These findings identify a context-dependent association rather than a causal or universally optimal collaboration structure, demonstrating how regional scientific collaboration portfolios relate to the evolution of publicly disclosed knowledge trajectories.

title: Shipment Monitoring, Allocation, and the Impact on Food Waste
abstract: Often advocated for the potential to reduce waste in fresh produce supply chains, sensor technologies enable firms to monitor the condition of each product unit and allocate them to markets at different transportation distances, thereby matching units with shorter shelf lives with closer markets. In this paper, we consider a firm purchasing and transporting a fresh produce product for sale in two destination markets. Postharvest processes cause a proportion of the product to be in risky condition, potentially becoming unsalable (“spoiled”) due to shelf-life deterioration during transportation. With monitoring technology, the firm first determines a purchase quantity and then decides how to allocate each unit (in either good or risky condition) between markets. We characterize the optimal allocation policies, which can be used to efficiently determine the optimal purchase quantity. Our analysis shows that such technology may inadvertently increase total waste by inducing larger purchase quantities; this increase is often, but not always, accompanied by a lower waste rate and improved distribution efficiency. As firms increasingly adopt monitoring technology for shipment allocation, additional policy and managerial attention may be required. Improvements in postharvest processes can strengthen the waste-reduction benefits of monitoring technology. Firms seeking to maintain their sustainability goals can capture most of the profit gains from monitoring by carefully moderating increases in purchase quantities. This paper was accepted by Jeannette Song, operations management. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07382 .

title: Retail on Wheels: A Time-Sensitive Traveling Salesman Problem
abstract: Rapid advancement in self-driving technology has brought mobile retail into the spotlight. Motivated by its potential, we present a model, theory, and insights into the operations of mobile retail, where a fleet of wheeled stores traverses a service region, selectively seeks locations in which to perch, and fulfills local customer demand. The goal of retailers is to strike a balance between perching and migrating to maximize total revenue. To dispatch such stores, retailers need to consider the following time-sensitive factors: (i) how busy the service is, (ii) how soon customers will arrive, and (iii) how quickly freshness decays. We propose and analyze a model that incorporates these factors into the classical traveling salesman problem (TSP), which we call the “time-sensitive TSP.” Using the continuous approximation approach, we derive the optimal revenue as well as the upper and lower bounds in the asymptotic regime as candidate locations increase to infinity. The tightness of the bounds is validated. Our analysis demonstrates that store mobility creates value by bringing proximity to customers. We further uncover the effects of these time-sensitive features on decision making. Specifically, the scaling relationship between revenue and fleet size is affected by customer tardiness and busyness. Busyness determines stores’ ability to expand their service, whereas tardiness affects how effectively stores can utilize the initial high-freshness period. These findings deepen our understanding of mobile retail operations. This paper was accepted by Karan Girotra, operations management. Funding: J. title: EXPRESS: Correcting omitted-variable bias without instruments: An ICA-based alternative to Gaussian copula methods
abstract: This paper proposes an instrument-free correction for omitted-variable bias and overcomes a key limitation of Gaussian copula control function (GCCF) approaches. Omitted-variable bias is the most common source of endogeneity in marketing, and many articles apply GCCF to address it. Yet GCCF require a nonlinear regressor-error relation, whereas textbooks assume linear, additive relationships between regressors and omitted variables. The authors prove that GCCF is biased in classical omitted-variable settings. Extant articles that address omitted-variables with GCCF also show language cues implicitly assuming linear relationships, which invalidate the use of GCCF. The proposed endogeneity correction is tailored to this prominent case, utilizing independent component analysis (ICA). It assumes a latent normally distributed component that additively influences both the endogenous regressor and the error. This can be interpreted as the sum of omitted variables, which, according to the Central Limit Theorem, add up to a normal distribution. Through ICA, this component is identified and extracted from the endogenous regressor, rendering the regression model free of endogeneity and enabling causal inference. The paper proves that the model is point-identified despite endogeneity due to omitted variables, that the proposed estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal, and that Jackknife resampling yields valid standard errors.

title: EXPRESS: The Role of Digital Ad Clutter in Ad Viewership and Memory
abstract: Advertisers face an increasingly cluttered digital ecosystem where customer attention matters. Despite this, the extent to which digital advertising clutter influences ad viewership remains unclear. This paper presents three separate eye-tracking experiments (subjects: N = 99, N = 250, and N = 575) using over a dozen custom-built web pages to better understand how digital ad clutter affects consumers’ viewing of digital ads. Across experiments, we show that increased clutter led consumers to allocate more attention to the overall advertising space and adjust how they distribute viewership across ad positions. A complementary survey revealed that clutter also reduced ad memory and recall for individual ads. We discuss the implications for advertisers and publishers regarding ad pricing and placement in crowded digital environments.

title: EXPRESS: Why are products so similar despite diverse consumer needs? The interplay between advertising and horizontal product differentiation
abstract: Firms are often less differentiated than standard price-competition models predict. We explain this gap by showing how firms can use informative or reminder advertising to soften competition. When firms choose locations, advertising, and prices endogenously, they may choose to soften price competition through limited advertising rather than greater product differentiation, allowing them to locate closer together while limiting price competition. This outcome of low advertising and central collocation is especially likely when advertising costs are high. We also observe that partially-differentiated equilibria, with one firm locating centrally and the other at an edge, and full differentiation, can each emerge under certain conditions. Thus, firms endogenously choose a mix of advertising and product differentiation to moderate price competition. Further, the shape of travel costs influences the equilibrium outcome. If the disutility from distance is highly convex, such as occurs when consumer preferences exhibit satisficing, central collocation becomes the unique equilibrium when more consumers are concentrated at the edge locations. However, when the disutility from distance is linear, having more customers located towards the edge locations makes collocation less likely. Overall, the interaction of advertising costs, consumer preferences, and location choices help explain why firms often forgo product differentiation.

title: Marketing misinformation in the age of AI
abstract: Abstract We shine a spotlight on marketing misinformation—claims about products and brands that contradict or distort verifiable facts. Misinformation may be created unintentionally or intentionally by companies, competitors, customers, or third parties seeking to harm companies or consumers. We focus on the role of AI in creating, obfuscating, and disseminating misinformation in the form of text, audio, images, and videos generated using large language models. This type of information can pose a substantial risk for brand safety. Consumers may be aware that AI can generate misinformation but may lack the ability to guard against it. We discuss how different stakeholders in the information ecosystem can help in the prevention and correction of misinformation and propose a future research agenda in this critical and fast‐growing area.

title: Pet-owner synchrony: Operationalization, application, and implications
abstract: Abstract Despite the pet industry’s significant economic and social importance, academic attention to this sector of the economy has been limited. Rather than focusing solely on the household demographics of pet ownership or the attitudinal components of the pet-owner relationship, we explore actual purchase decisions of pet owners. In this study, we examine pet-owner synchrony, a behavioral operationalization of pet-owner relationships that is grounded in attachment theory, anthropomorphism, and the extended self. Utilizing scanner data from 875,853 market baskets including 23 million transactions collected from a regional supermarket chain, we analyze cross-category co-occurrence patterns within shopping baskets. Our analysis reveals affinities, or parallels, in pet owners’ purchases of health and wellness products and hedonic products for both themselves and their pets, which we attribute to pet-owner synchrony. We identify two moderators that influence the strength of pet-owner synchrony: pet type (cat versus dog) and the presence of young children in the household. In addition, we evaluate how basket size, holidays, and price elasticities impact pet-owner synchrony. Our findings deliver useful insights into pet-owner relationships, have direct implications for retail and manufacturing managers, and yield recommendations for public policy.

Branch-and-Price for the Team Orienteering Problem with Time Windows and Bivariate Time-Varying Profit
abstract: Motivated by multiple real-world applications, this study investigates the team orienteering problem with time windows and bivariate time-varying profit (TOPTW-BTP), where the profit collected at each node is modeled as a nonlinear function of both the arrival time and the service duration. We model the problem on a time-expanded network and introduce the concept of the bivariate-time (BT) arc, proving that dominated BT arcs can be systematically eliminated to reduce the solution space. To capture diverse real-world temporal profit patterns, we consider three types of arrival-time profit functions, monotonic (typically decreasing), concave, and others (e.g., bimodal), and discuss tailored modeling approaches for each case to avoid unnecessary arrival-time discretization. Especially for the concave case, we propose a novel route extension method that exploits the structural properties of concavity to mathematically formalize the extension as direct functional additions, thereby achieving a compact representation. This method is also applicable to related problems such as vehicle routing with time windows and convex node costs. A branch-and-price framework is developed to solve the TOPTW-BTP. Computational experiments show that the proposed algorithm efficiently solves instances with up to 100 nodes across all three types of arrival-time profit function, with the theoretical simplification in the concave case naturally leading to a more streamlined implementation than the state-of-the-art approach. title: Online Decisions with (Biased) Offline Data
abstract: Making Better Decisions with Imperfect Historical Data Historical data can provide valuable information for online decision making, but its usefulness may be limited when the environment has changed. In “Online Decisions with (Biased) Offline Data,” Ahn, Zhang, and Zhang study how firms can combine potentially biased offline data with newly collected online observations in two canonical operations management problems: dynamic inventory decisions and dynamic pricing. The authors develop two online learning policies that balance the benefits of historical information against the risk of relying on data from a different distribution. The soft-switch policy automatically adjusts the reliance on offline and online data without requiring prior knowledge of the degree of bias. The hard-switch policy instead uses information about the magnitude of the distributional shift to determine when to rely primarily on online data. Both policies achieve optimal regret up to a logarithmic factor, whereas the analysis quantifies how the value of offline data depends on its size and bias.

title: Operations Management in the Sharing Economy: Advances, Challenges, and Opportunities
abstract: The rapid growth of the sharing economy over the past decade has changed many industries in profound ways. The innovative business models that have emerged in the sharing economy present unique opportunities as well as challenges, which have attracted a significant amount of attention from researchers in the operations management field. In this paper, we discuss the advances, challenges, and opportunities for research on operations management in the sharing economy. We divide sharing economy into eight categories: Ride Sharing, Space Sharing, Bike Sharing, Vehicle Sharing, Group Buying, Crowdfunding, Freelancing, and Last-Mile Delivery. For each business category, we identify the gaps and current challenges in the existing literature, discuss emerging industry trends and research topics, and suggest several future research directions. Our goal is to stimulate discussion and ideas about future studies in this area.

title: A Continuous-Time Model of Subscription and Repeat Purchase
abstract: Problem definition: We present a continuous-time model of consumers’ joint decisions of membership subscription and repeat purchase. A consumer pays a flow membership fee; her valuation follows a Brownian motion, purchase needs arrive via a Poisson process, and she chooses whether to buy and when to unsubscribe. The model is analytically tractable thanks to the connection between consumer lifetime and hitting time of Brownian motions. Methodology/results: Consumers’ unsubscription decision solves an optimal-stopping problem with a closed-form valuation cutoff; purchase occurs when valuation exceeds the transaction price. These thresholds generate three fluid consumer modes—buyer, tracker, and churner. We find that consumers who are about to terminate subscription tend to purchase less frequently, and who are currently subscribing are more likely to continue subscription. This endogenous customer loyalty is captured by a one-parameter retention formula [Formula: see text], which can accommodate rapid early attrition and an asymptotic slow decay. Managerial implications: For empirical estimation, we cast latent-valuation filtering as a heat-diffusion problem and develop a kernel-iteration likelihood approximation with vanishing discretization errors. Three empirical studies that feature two distinct firm-customer relationships demonstrate that our model performs on par with or better than existing models. Based on the model estimates, firms can infer consumers’ latent engagement and churn risk from purchase histories and devise the optimal package of membership fee and transaction price.

title: Response efficiency versus response customization: An examination of firms’ responses to platform-empowered group complaints
abstract: The rise of group complaints on digital platforms, where consumers can publicly voice collective concerns, presents significant challenges for firms’ service recovery operations. Prior research assessing service operations on digital platforms has focused primarily on individual complaints, and less is known about how firms respond to platform-empowered (PE) group complaints. We examine this question through the lens of a trade-off between response efficiency and response customization and argue that this trade-off evolves as group complaints develop over time. Based on a large-scale dataset from Tousu, a leading complaint platform in China, we find that group complaints paradoxically increase response time and decrease empathy and explanation in firms’ responses. Further analyses indicate that these effects depend on dynamic group size and dynamic need diversity. When dynamic need diversity is low, larger groups are associated with more standardized, efficiency-oriented responses, whereas when dynamic need diversity is high, larger groups are associated with slower but more customized responses. These findings extend research on service operations by showing how PE group complaints reshape firms’ complaint handling. Our study also provides operational guidance for managing group complaints more effectively.

title: Multi-self presentation and knowledge contribution in platform operations: Evidence from a natural experiment
abstract: Operations of online user-generated content (UGC) platforms often involve tackling under-provision , wherein users lack motivation to contribute sufficient content. We study a novel design deployed to address this issue: the integration of a proprietary social feature that allows users to post casual free-form content (e.g., casual social content) alongside standard formal content on the platform. Leveraging a quasi-experiment on a large Chinese online knowledge-sharing platform, we assess the effects of integrating such a social feature on users’ formal knowledge contribution (i.e., writing answers to others’ questions ). Using difference-in-differences (DiD) analyses paired with various matching strategies, such as propensity score matching and look-ahead propensity score matching, we find that users who adopt and frequently use the feature (i.e., high adopters) show a stronger incentive to contribute answers without compromising quality. These results are further validated by a set of robustness checks. Further mediation analysis suggests that such a complementary effect might be because of two mechanisms related to the integrated social feature’s multi-self presentation function: first, the new feature increases high adopters’ engagement on the platform and leads them to consume more knowledge content, which in turn facilitates knowledge contribution; second, high adopters receive more social recognition benefits by building a more complete self through the integrated social feature, and such increased social recognition benefits further motivate more subsequent content contribution. Moreover, employing a text-mining approach to assess the semantic similarity between users’ casual social content and their formal knowledge contributions, we find that the complementary effect is amplified for high adopters whose casual posts remain more closely connected to their formal knowledge domain (i.e., are more semantically aligned with their formal knowledge). Our results have novel implications for platform design and operations to motivate users to contribute valuable content.

title: EXPRESS: Mind the Cost of Disturbance: Firm-Level Supply Chain Risk and the Bank Loan Cost
abstract: This study investigates whether and how supply chain risk, a core operational vulnerability, is priced in financial credit markets. Using a novel text-based firm-level measure, we show that elevated supply chain risk leads to higher loan interest spreads. Exploiting natural disasters as exogenous shocks to production networks, we provide causal evidence that shocks increase perceived supply chain fragility and, in turn, raise borrowing costs. These effects are amplified when lenders face greater private-information deficiency, and are further strengthened when external information production is more intensive — the former heightening lenders’ concern over supply chain exposure, the latter enhancing their capacity to recognize and price it. Critically, lenders treat supply chain fragility as a form of credit risk: firms with higher supply chain risk face increased default risk, and firms whose production networks are struck by supplier disasters face a higher probability of covenant violation and tighter covenant restrictions, signaling lenders’ anticipation of repayment difficulties. Our findings highlight a new financial consequence of operational risk, showing that supply chain disruption directly affects corporate financing outcomes.
topics: Supply Chain Resilience and Risk Management

title: EXPRESS: Pricing and Information Provision in Service Platforms with Heterogeneous Customers
abstract: Service platforms frequently employ virtual queues where customers have differing sensitivities to wait times and cannot see their precise positions in line. In these settings, providers often disclose waiting-time information to influence customers' decisions on whether to join or balk. A natural benchmark is to report the long-term average waiting time, yet whether this deterministic disclosure policy is optimal remains unclear when both pricing and customer participation are endogenous. This study develops a stylized theoretical framework to explore the joint structure of pricing and waiting-time information disclosure for service providers managing diverse customers in a virtual queue. The provider decides on both the service price and the waiting-time disclosure policy within a rational-expectations framework. Our findings reveal that the optimal disclosure strategy is captured by scaled Rademacher distributions, meaning at most two distinct announcement values are required. This reduces a complex infinite-dimensional problem to a more manageable finite-dimensional optimization task. Leveraging this framework, we derive the optimal strategies for pricing and disclosure, identifying scenarios where variability in announced waiting times is beneficial. Our analysis shows that noise is advantageous when customers can handle uncertain wait-time signals or initially perceive the service as quick. The optimal level of noise correlates with system congestion, offering the greatest benefits when there is a notable disparity between perceived and actual congestion levels. This provides significant advantages when disclosing waiting times with noise. These findings offer actionable insights for service platforms, guiding them in creating cohesive strategies that encompass pricing, information disclosure, and service configuration, ultimately enhancing customer experience and operational efficiency.

title: EXPRESS: Valuation Bottlenecks: Why Isn’t a Better Business Enough for a Higher Market Capitalization?
abstract: Firms often improve operations, disclosure, governance, or financing capacity without an immediate and proportional market-capitalization response. Could a single unresolved concern limit the market's response to improvements elsewhere in the firm? Classical multifactor and machine-learning models ask which risks or characteristics explain or predict returns. We ask whether the relatively weakest among several coexisting firm conditions receives disproportionate valuation weight. We model equity value as the lower envelope of lens-specific valuations. A hard minimum makes one lens locally binding; a soft minimum assigns continuous, state-dependent weights. We use exploratory factor analysis on 268 accounting characteristics to construct five firm-state lenses, with membership and weights determined by the loading structure rather than by an economic taxonomy, and rank each lens within industry, size, and quarter peers. We document a weakest lens effect : beyond the additive effects of all five lens ranks, a firm's weakest lens carries an incremental association with next-quarter returns, and it survives saturated joint rank-quintile controls. Gating the test at the bottom decile and then the bottom quintile of the peer distribution, the association is concentrated among firms whose weakest lens is weak against peers and not merely lowest within the firm. In baseline soft-min specifications, it fades steadily as the gate is widened. We then investigate whether analyst attention may help explain this pattern. We use large language models on 1.7 million earnings-call questions and find that, in baseline specifications, the weakest lens attracts a larger share of questions, especially when it is also weak among peers; this cross-sectional alignment is consistent with an attention channel as one possible explanation for the observed return pattern. The framework offers managers seeking to maximize market capitalization a new perspective on prioritizing scarce managerial attention.

title: EXPRESS: From Institutional Expansion to Exposure-Driven Co-Evolution: Reinterpreting “Operations and Supply Chain Management in China”
abstract: This paper builds on and reinterprets Wu (2026a,b), which offers a comprehensive account of the rapid institutional, educational, and research development of Operations and Supply Chain Management (OSCM) in China. While the Institutional–Dynamic–Organizational (IDO) framework effectively captures domestic structural transformation, it under-theorizes a critical external driver of this evolution: international knowledge exposure and collaboration. To address this gap, we complement Wu’s analysis with a bibliometric study of published articles in Production and Operations Management from 1992 to 2026. The evidence shows that China’s growing presence in OSCM research is overwhelmingly collaboration-mediated, with China–U.S. co-authorship constituting the dominant channel of integration. The rise of China in top-tier OSCM journals is therefore not primarily an autonomous national trajectory, but a structurally embedded phenomenon within global co-authorship networks. Our findings suggest that China’s OSCM evolution cannot be fully explained by domestic institutional expansion, policy support, or educational scaling alone. Instead, it reflects a broader process of exposure-driven co-evolution within a globally integrated knowledge system. In this system, international collaboration is not merely a byproduct of scientific development but a central mechanism shaping the structure and trajectory of global OSCM knowledge production.

title: Economic Inequality Reduces Sustainable Consumption: Cross-National and Experimental Evidence and Psychological Mechanisms
abstract: Abstract This research investigates the relationship between economic inequality and sustainable consumption, highlighting how socioeconomic disparities shape consumer behavior. Across three studies—using secondary data from 20 countries, a vignette experiment, and UK survey data—we provide empirical evidence that individuals report lower levels of sustainable consumption when inequality levels are objectively high, perceived as high, or experimentally manipulated as high. This effect can be explained through norm activation theory: As inequality rises, consumers feel less responsible for environmental damage and are less aware of the environmental impact of their consumption choices. These dynamics weaken sustainability-oriented personal norms and, in turn, reduce sustainable consumption. Our findings suggest that reducing economic inequality can significantly enhance sustainable consumption.
