title: Media-Manager Sentiment Gap and Stock Returns: Evidence from China
Artificial intelligence and venture capital: Revisiting sourcing, selection, and nurturing activities
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Venture capital (VC) is an information‐intensive form of entrepreneurial finance conducted under extreme uncertainty. Investors must originate promising opportunities, select ventures with sparse and strategically disclosed information, and monitor and support firms after investment. Prior research documents both formal mechanisms (e.g., staged financing, syndication) and informal mechanisms built on referrals, reputation, and constant interaction. Geographic and social proximity enable these mechanisms by lowering the cost of obtaining contextual information and coordinating action. We develop a mechanism‐based account of how data and Artificial Intelligence (AI) reconfigure this established model. Our framework yields propositions on geographic dispersion in sourcing, portfolio selection, and the distinct effects of AI on monitoring versus value‐added support. It also identifies boundary conditions associated with institutional setting and heterogeneous AI adoption. Managerial Summary For venture capital firms, AI is not a single tool and adoption is not a binary choice. A fund may use data systems to identify founders, machine‐learning models to organize deal flow, generative AI to summarize diligence materials, or analytics to monitor portfolio companies. Each application changes a different part of the VC process. In sourcing, AI can widen the funnel beyond warm introductions and local ecosystems, especially in sectors such as software and e‐commerce where hiring, product, and customer signals are visible. In selection, AI can make diligence faster and more consistent, but models trained on past investments may favor ventures that resemble previously funded companies and may miss novel opportunities for which historical analogues are weak. In post‐investment activity, continuous operational data can partly replace physical presence for monitoring, while value‐add support such as customer introductions, recruiting, strategy advice, and founder coaching remain relationship‐intensive. The practical implication is a task‐level approach: automate codifiable search and processing, retain independent human judgment where uncertainty is fundamental, and use AI to strengthen rather than erode trusted investor–founder relationships. Funds also face organizational choices about building proprietary infrastructure, buying external tools, or combining the two. The appropriate configuration depends on data access, strategy, scale, and the activity in which the fund seeks advantage.

title: Entrepreneurial theorizing with generative artificial intelligence
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Whether large language model (LLM) assistance changes how entrepreneurs construct theories remains unclear. On the one hand, LLMs may help entrepreneurs build more developed causal structures and surface diverse information that supports the formulation of distinctive theories. On the other hand, LLMs may steer causal structures toward conventional forms and discourage the counterintuitive reasoning needed to develop distinctive theories. In a within‐subject experiment with 199 participants theorizing both with and without LLM assistance, we find no significant average treatment effect on either structural or content properties. However, this null average effect masks a redistribution effect, where LLM assistance supplemented theorizing when unaided theories were less developed or distinctive but displaced participants' own theorizing when their theories were already more developed or distinctive. Managerial Summary Large language models (LLMs) can help entrepreneurs develop business ideas by surfacing knowledge across domains and sharpening causal logic. At the same time, LLMs may also push reasoning toward conventional patterns and away from the counterintuitive ideas that are a source of breakthrough opportunities. In a study of 199 participants theorizing with and without LLM assistance, we find that LLMs supported the development of causal structure and content distinctiveness when unaided theories were less developed or distinctive, whereas they had the opposite effect when those theories were already more developed or distinctive. This suggests that while LLMs can scaffold entrepreneurs still developing their theories, greater caution is warranted for those whose theories are already more developed or distinctive, as assistance may diminish those properties.

title: Contested credibility: Public perceptions of scientists as experts
abstract: Science is widely embraced as an important prerequisite for innovation, and there is widespread support for public investment in science on that basis. However, it remains more contested whether and when science is recognized as a relevant source of expertise in contemporary debates beyond the academic sphere. Drawing on nationally representative survey panels from two European countries (the United Kingdom and Sweden), we investigate whether scientists are perceived as more credible senders of messages regarding societal challenges compared with attribution to other types of expert groups (government, businesspersons, and issue advocates). Evidence from a conjoint analysis paints a rather bleak picture: scientists' credibility is only superior to that of government officials, but not businesspersons or issue advocates. We furthermore find that scientists are more credible when communicating technological issues than non-technological ones. This pattern can be traced back to three types of perceived sources of distrust (vested interest, partisanship and irrelevance) that are activated more strongly for non-technological issues. The same three sources of distrust also underpin the general credibility disadvantage of scientists as experts. Implications for our understanding of the social contract of science are discussed.

title: Event System Theory: A Decade of Progress and a Future of Potential
abstract: Published 10 years ago, event system theory (EST; Morgeson, Mitchell & Liu, 2015) has become a highly influential organizational theory. EST consists of a complex of three interacting event components: event strength, event space, and event time. It has been used by scholars across domains in a variety of different ways and serves as a key catalyst for event-oriented research and theory. In this article, we reflect upon the development of EST and discuss the impact it has had on the field. We then identify the different ways EST has been used, offer suggestions for studying events, and discuss all the work that still needs to be done.

title: AI-Driven Human Task Substitution: Evidence from Google Translate and ChatGPT
abstract: We examine how different generations of artificial intelligence (AI) substitute for human knowledge worker tasks, leveraging two sequential natural experiments in the translation industry. We study the introduction of Google Neural Machine Translation (GNMT), a predictive, task-specific AI, as well as ChatGPT, a broad, general-purpose generative AI, in a major online labor market. Distinguishing between analytical tasks (regular translations) and intuitive tasks (transcreations, which require creative and cultural adaptation), we estimate difference-in-differences models on transaction-level data from 2016 to 2017 and 2022 to 2023. We find that GNMT reduced the demand for analytical tasks by economically meaningful magnitudes, while having no detectable effect on intuitive tasks. By contrast, ChatGPT produced substantially larger and more uniform reductions for both analytical and intuitive tasks, indicating a marked expansion in the scope and magnitude of AI substitution. By comparing these two technological shocks within the same labor market, we show that conclusions about which types of human work are resilient to automation do not straightforwardly generalize from predictive to generative AI. This paper was accepted by Joshua Gans, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06740 .
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality
Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

title: Systemically Important Banks and Loan Performance: Evidence from India
abstract: We examine whether designating banks as systemically important affects loan performance in an emerging-market setting where such banks are large domestic institutions and market imperfections make monitoring crucial for loan performance. Using loan-level data and the staggered designation of banks as Domestic Systemically Important Banks (DSIBs) in India, we find that loan performance deteriorates following DSIB designation. The evidence points to bank-level moral hazard as the underlying mechanism: DSIBs reduce postorigination monitoring and weaken loan recovery efforts. Borrowers respond accordingly, exhibiting poorer financial health and loan repayment, particularly on loans extended by DSIBs. This paper was accepted by Jan Bouwens, accounting. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03238 .

title: Why Do We Discriminate? Directional Beliefs and Biased Information Processing
abstract: Identifying the cause of discrimination is crucial to designing effective policies and to understanding discrimination dynamics. This paper provides a potential link between existing models of taste-based and statistical discrimination by studying directional belief formation through biased information search and processing. By selectively acquiring and processing information, individuals form directional beliefs and consequently discriminate based on these beliefs. Through a series of experiments in which individuals endogenously acquire and process various signals, I document discrimination stemming from directional beliefs and demonstrate important differences in how it manifests compared with taste-based and statistical discrimination. Finally, I show that limiting individuals’ scope to interpret information reduces such discrimination. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: Financial support from the Sustainable Architecture for Finance in Europe Experiment Center Frankfurt [Grant 232406], the Interdisciplinary Public Policy Mainz [Grant A2021011], and the Mainzer Wissenschaftsstiftung is gratefully acknowledged. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01818 .

title: Music Marketing with Generative AI
abstract: The multibillion-dollar music industry faces severe content creation bottlenecks, making multimedia marketing assets prohibitively costly for smaller artists. This practice paper introduces a Marketing Asset Generation Engine (MAGE) that can produce over 700 million video ad variations reflecting each artist’s visual identity using only a music track’s audio and album cover as inputs. Collaborating with one of the world’s largest music labels, we conduct four preregistered field studies with over 11 million impressions across 75 campaigns for 33 music tracks on TikTok and Meta to validate MAGE. First, pooled across studies, MAGE-generated ads significantly outperform human-designed ads on TikTok with on average 26% higher click-through rates and 10% higher engagement, while we do not detect statistically significant performance differences on Meta, all at 98% lower production cost. Second, neither marketing professionals nor laypeople can reliably identify winning ads such that random sampling of MAGE’s outputs performs as well as human-curated selections. In contrast, an AI-in-the-loop system trained on past performance data can predict pre-launch which MAGE-generated ads will perform best for specific audience segments. These findings demonstrate that generative AI democratizes music marketing by making effective, on-brand video ads accessible at scale.

title: Externalities of Responsible Investments
abstract: ABSTRACT We develop a model to study the efficiency of socially responsible investing (SRI) as a mechanism to control firms' externalities. When SRI is not too popular, responsible investors favor strategies that lead to a concentration of SRI in a subset of firms in the economy. This concentration can mitigate coordination issues in adopting green technologies, but it can also crowd out the green investments of excluded firms and increase the price of green products. In equilibrium, responsible investors continue to favor concentration even as SRI becomes more popular, and concentrate the most when concentration is least desirable.

title: Disagreement of disagreement
abstract: We show that leading investor disagreement proxies have near-zero cross-correlation – making disagreement pricing inferences challenging. We develop a frictionless model that generates overpricing from latent disagreement, jointly rationalizes major proxies, and generates new testable predictions. Equilibrium interrelationships motivate a new disagreement measure, DIS, which is more predictive of returns cross-sectionally than major proxies and more consistently predictive across macroeconomic regimes. We provide evidence that the friction-based channel of Miller (1977) and a frictionless mechanism coexist and are empirically separable. DIS also provides a micro-founded, disagreement-based account of the IVOL puzzle, absorbing IVOL’s predictability while revealing its regime and friction dependence.

title: Learning Optimal Classification Trees Robust to Distribution Shifts
abstract: We consider the problem of learning classification trees that are robust to distribution shifts between training and testing/deployment data. This problem arises frequently in high stakes settings such as public health and social work where data is often collected using self-reported surveys which are highly sensitive to e.g., the framing of the questions, the time when and place where the survey is conducted, and the level of comfort the interviewee has in sharing information with the interviewer. We propose a method for learning optimal robust classification trees based on mixed-integer robust optimization technology. In particular, we demonstrate that the problem of learning an optimal robust tree can be cast as a single-stage mixed-integer robust optimization problem with a highly nonlinear and discontinuous objective. We reformulate this problem equivalently as a two-stage linear robust optimization problem for which we devise a tailored solution procedure based on constraint generation. We evaluate the performance of our approach on numerous publicly available datasets, and compare the performance to a regularized, non-robust optimal tree. We show an increase of up to 12.48 percentage points in worst-case accuracy and of up to 4.85 percentage points in average-case accuracy across several datasets and distribution shifts from using our robust solution in comparison to the non-robust one.

title: Competition for Customer Attention is Creating Oversupply Pockets in US Micromobility
abstract: We present analytical and empirical arguments that competition over a nearly homogeneous service forces operators to oversupply scooters in urban centers. First, using deployment and ride data from operator APIs and city transportation departments, as well as telemetry data from one of the top three U.S. operators, we estimate average daily scooter utilization across nine major U.S. cities at 3.9%—half the 7.7% minimum utilization target set by transportation departments. Second, using a parsimonious game-theoretic model, we argue that if riders choose among available scooters roughly at random (e.g., the closest one), then in equilibrium all operators need to inflate their fleet sizes to preserve their market shares. Third, using granular data on riders’ choice sets and choices from Kansas City, MO, we provide evidence that these choices are indeed roughly random. Fourth, using our structurally estimated game-theoretic model, we find that in Kansas City, MO: (i) there is a 406% oversupply of scooters, (ii) the interaction between rider choice and competition accounts for 81% of this oversupply, and (iii) if the transportation department issued one more operator permit, oversupply would increase by an additional 82 pp. We conclude that transportation departments should be frugal with the number of permits they issue, and should welcome the consolidation of the scooter market.

title: Stochastic Dual Dynamic Programming for Log-linear Autoregressive Uncertainty in the Right-hand Side
abstract: We consider the generation of cuts in stochastic dual dynamic programming (SDDP) for multistage stochastic linear programming problems with stagewise dependent uncertainty in the right-hand side described by a nonlinear autoregressive process. We first derive cut formulas for the general nonlinear autoregressive process. For these general cuts, the computational tractability becomes a major challenge for SDDP-type algorithms. We are, however, able to develop tractable closed-form cut formulas for the special case of log-linear autoregressive processes. The obtained cuts are in general non-convex in the history of the stochastic process, but still linear in all decision variables, and thus can be directly incorporated into the subproblems in SDDP without compromising their linearity. If solvers do not allow for this, our formulas can be used to adapt the intercept of a given cut to a scenario at hand in a computationally tractable way. In this sense, cuts generated for one specific scenario are shared with other scenarios. Our findings are supported by a computational study of a hydrothermal scheduling problem, which demonstrates a favorable performance of our proposed version of SDDP compared to approaches from the literature.

title: Operations management for sustainable development and public policy making
abstract: Public policy making often faces challenges in implementation due to a lack of attention to operational realities. Operations management (OM) research, with its strong empirical component and focus on detailed model-based mechanisms, offers unique insights for successful policy execution. This paper explores the synergies between economics, development economics, and OM in addressing public policy implementation, arguing that OM’s process-level understanding, empirical rigor, and focus on operational feasibility can enhance policy design and evaluation. We illustrate this potential through examples from sustainability and social development, demonstrating how OM can bridge the gap between economic policy insights and operational execution.

title: Theorizing future phenomena: Metaverse, wearables, and humanoids
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We propose that entrepreneurship and strategy research can develop theory about phenomena of the future rather than only explain those of the past. Research has potential for practical relevance when researchers make claims towards applications to decisions practitioners have yet to make. Theory grounded in a world that may differ from the observed world can be built through a process of extrapolation from technological trends, a practice utilized by entrepreneurs and science fiction authors alike. Assuming advances in artificial intelligence, we apply this process to three emerging phenomena: governing scarcity in metaverse virtual worlds, redesigning organizations around pervasive monitoring via wearable devices, and allocating the intellectual property rights of humanoid robots. We argue that embracing theory that speaks to the future can enhance the practical and educational relevance of management research. Managerial Summary Assuming artificial intelligence continues to improve, we highlight three impending phenomena poised to transform conventional approaches to entrepreneurship and strategy. First, in metaverse virtual worlds, managers must manage resources governed by artificial scarcity. Second, with wearable devices allowing continuous monitoring, managers must consider alternative structures for vertical hierarchy and horizontal collaboration. Third, deployment of humanoid robots will complicate intellectual property rights and asset ownership. We propose that scholarship towards developing theoretical frameworks addressing these and other phenomena of the future will be relevant to both managers and students.

title: Value creation and capture in artificial intelligence‐enabled ecosystems
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We develop an ecosystem perspective on AI‐enabled value creation, grounded in AI's characteristics as a general‐purpose technology. We consider that AI can support multiple value propositions realized through distinct but interconnected ecosystems. Within this structure, AI innovators face choices concerning which value propositions to support, whether to pursue them through general‐purpose or specialized offers, and whether to make those offers open or closed. Users, in turn, are strategic actors facing choices among alternative ecosystem configurations of focal offers and complements through which the same value proposition might be realized. These choices by innovators and users may alter ecosystem roles and competitive relationships over time. We conclude by outlining research opportunities for strategy and innovation scholars examining how firms create and capture value in AI‐enabled ecosystems. Managerial Summary Value creation with AI depends not only on the technology's capability but on the actors whose combined contributions deliver a value proposition. AI supports many value propositions, each through its own ecosystem, with some elements shared across them. AI innovators choose which value propositions to serve, whether to do so through general‐purpose or specialized offers, and whether to make their offers open or proprietary. User firms choose among alternative configurations of offers and complements through which the same value proposition can be realized. These choices may shift the competitive relationships between actors within an ecosystem over time. This perspective surfaces questions of relevance for scholars and practitioners regarding value creation and capture with AI.

title: Training and productivity in micro-firms
abstract: This paper examines the effect of training on productivity of micro-firms, defined in official statistics as firms with less than 10 employees. While training may represent a crucial mode of knowledge accumulation in micro-firms, which usually lack resources or structure to devote to formal innovation activities, the specificities of micro-businesses suggest that training may even be detrimental to productivity of this category of firms. Yet, the received wisdom that training should foster their productivity, as it does in larger firms, remains un-tested, mainly due to difficulties in previous literature to analyze micro-firms separately from the wider groups of small or small-medium enterprises. Exploiting a unique administrative panel dataset that records training expenses of a large sample of micro-firms located in three Italian regions, we address whether micro-firms which train enjoy a productivity premium vis-a-vis micro-firms that do not. Our main finding, controlling for endogeneity of training via Inverse Probability Weighted Regression Adjustment methods, combined with firm fixed-effects, is a positive and sizable average treatment effect of training, stable across a series of robustness checks and heterogeneity analysis.
topics: Human Resource Development and Performance Evaluation

title: Comment Letters, Connected Investors, and Corporate Bond Issuance
abstract: Using a proprietary data set that documents corporate bond issuances in China, we find that bond regulators’ comment letters (CLs) on issuers’ public disclosures generally target opaque firms and reduce bond issuance success. We also find, however, that connected investors—financial institutions with prior business relationships with the issuers—purchase a relatively larger share of bond issuances from CL recipients than from non-CL recipients, and this greater participation contributes to overpricing. Further analysis shows that connected investors support CL recipients because they possess superior private information and obtain private benefits from their connections. This paper was accepted by Ranjani Krishnan, accounting. Funding: R. Zhang acknowledges financial support from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada [Grant 31-R833984]. Supplemental Material: The internet appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07607 .

title: Unintended Regulatory Spillovers: The Impact of Bank Regulatory Oversight on Environmental Enforcement
abstract: ABSTRACT We explore whether bank regulatory oversight affects the ability of environmental enforcement to reduce industrial emissions. A major objective of environmental enforcement is to reduce industrial emissions by encouraging firms to employ greener production processes and technologies. However, such changes often require external financing obtained from banks, and prior research shows that regulatory oversight of banks can affect bank lending. We find that, on average, the reduction in air pollution in response to county‐level environmental enforcement is attenuated in counties exposed to increased bank regulatory oversight, as measured by severe enforcement actions. Furthermore, we show that the negative impact of bank regulatory oversight on small business lending to affected counties is the likely mechanism behind this on‐average effect. However, when bank regulatory oversight targets banks with stronger capitalization, we find that the negative effect of bank regulatory oversight on environmental enforcement is mitigated. Collectively, our findings suggest that bank regulation has a nuanced effect on the extent to which environmental enforcement reduces emissions, indicating that one regulator's mission can impact the objectives of another.

title: How do audit committee members' and audit partners' communication styles jointly influence client managers’ negotiation behavior?
abstract: Auditor-client negotiations over contentious accounting issues can shape reported financial outcomes, yet little is known about how communication dynamics between audit committee (AC) members and auditors influence client negotiation behavior. We conduct an experiment in which experienced financial executives, assuming the role of chief financial officer, negotiate a disputed inventory obsolescence allowance with a simulated audit partner in the presence of an AC member; the AC member's distributive communication style (offensive vs. defensive) and the audit partner's reflective empathy (high vs. low) are manipulated between participants. Drawing on relational framing theory in interpersonal communication, we predict and find that a distributive-offensive AC communication style leads clients to establish their reporting positions and concede less to the auditor's proposed adjustment, unless it is accompanied by high reflective empathy from the audit partner, which neutralizes this resistance. This pattern emerges in the client's initial negotiation position and persists through the final negotiated allowance. Our findings suggest that auditors can use empathetic communication as a strategic tool to defuse the competitive posture that an assertive governance signal may provoke. Overall, our results provide insights into how AC members' and auditors' communication styles jointly shape client negotiation behavior, highlighting the importance of communication strategies in achieving effective audit negotiation outcomes.

title: Would a Balanced PCAOB Inspection Approach Increase Auditors' Use of Innovative Audit Procedures?
abstract: ABSTRACT Prior research criticizes PCAOB inspection reports for focusing solely on audit deficiencies, arguing that this encourages auditors to pursue traditional procedures to demonstrate compliance with standards rather than procedures that maximize audit quality. We contribute to this debate by examining whether the PCAOB's approach discourages auditors from considering innovative audit procedures (that are potentially more effective), since they are, by definition, less standard. We compare the PCAOB's current inspection approach (which focuses on reporting audit deficiencies) to a balanced inspection approach that discloses examples of audit strengths as well as deficiencies discovered during inspections. We predict and find that when the risk of material misstatement (RMM) is moderate, a balanced inspection approach leads auditors to consider the potential effectiveness of innovative audit procedures to a greater extent, ultimately prioritizing more of them in audit plans. Our findings contribute to both research and practice by enhancing our understanding of ways to encourage audit innovation and ultimately improve overall audit quality.

title: Could That Happen to Me? Auditor Response When Colleagues Are Named in Lawsuits
abstract: ABSTRACT Litigation risk is an important source of motivation for auditors to conduct high‐quality audits, but theory suggests that certain lawsuits will have a more salient disciplining effect on auditor behavior. To this end, we identify lawsuits naming an individual partner as a co‐defendant along with the audit firm. We then examine how these lawsuits affect subsequent behavior of other auditors in the office of the sued partner. Relative to lawsuits naming only the firm, our results indicate that lawsuits naming individual partners as co‐defendants are significant office‐level events that motivate a meaningful response from non‐sued audit partners in the form of higher quality and fees on existing clients and more careful client portfolio management. These results have practical implications about how auditor litigation incentivizes individual auditors to fulfill their professional duties. For regulators and audit firms seeking to promote audit quality, these findings highlight the disciplining effect of auditors' concern for their personal reputation and litigation exposure. Furthermore, audit committees, clients, and investors may observe elevated audit quality, effort, and fees following partner‐level litigation in the local office.

title: Risk, Specialization, and Covered‐Interest Parity
abstract: ABSTRACT Prevailing theories of financial intermediation assume an integrated financial sector with frictionless risk‐sharing. However, we identify substantial risk‐sharing frictions linked to intermediary specialization using currency derivatives markets as a laboratory. Using confidential supervisory data covering $25 trillion in daily bank exposures, we document imperfect hedging in banks' FX‐swap intermediation: banks rarely hedge their synthetic dollar lending with maturity‐matched foreign safe assets. Intermediaries specialize in markets in which they have expertise in managing the associated exposures, giving rise to cross‐market variation in deviations from covered‐interest parity. Our results highlight the importance of intermediary specialization and its impact on risk premia.

title: Charitable capital allocation: Evidence from private foundations
Firm Heterogeneity and the Impact of Immigration: Evidence from German Establishments
Buying Data from Consumers: The Impact of Monitoring in U.S. Auto Insurance
Community-Oriented Market Design for Nonprofit Resource Exchange
abstract: Unlocking Value Through Nonprofit Resource Sharing Nonprofit organizations often operate under tight budgets while idle equipment, unused space, and shareable skills and expertise are frequently underutilized, with existing resource exchanges in the nonprofit sector limited to bilateral barter or relatively homogeneous resources. In “Community-Oriented Market Design for Nonprofit Resource Exchange,” Huang et al. propose Sharing With a Purpose (SWAP), a resource-sharing system that enables nonprofits to exchange heterogeneous resources without monetary payments. SWAP combines an auction-based process, SWAPcredit valuation, and integer optimization to facilitate multilateral exchanges, allowing nonprofits to obtain needed resources by contributing resources of their own. The authors implement this market design through the SWAP Hub, a digital platform deployed with nonprofit communities in multiple regions. Through repeated exchange episodes, participating organizations have shared not only physical assets but also a wide range of skills, services, and expertise, including marketing, management, event planning, and organizational development. The study demonstrates how innovative market design can unlock latent value in community resources, alleviate resource constraints, and encourage new connections and collaboration among nonprofit organizations.

title: Optimality of Public Persuasion for Single-Good Allocation
abstract: When Sharing the Same Information Is Optimal Should a school advisor tailor recommendation letters to different employers or share the same information with everyone? Similar questions arise in start-up fundraising and biotech partnerships. In “Optimality of Public Persuasion for Single-Good Allocation,” Chen and Qi study how a sender can strategically disclose information when allocating an indivisible good to at most one self-interested receiver. The sender may send tailored private messages to individual receivers or publicly broadcast the same information to everyone. Surprisingly, the authors show that, when the sender has a known preference ordering over receivers, public persuasion is optimal even if receivers can subsequently communicate and share information. The optimal public mechanism can be derived from a simpler first-best allocation problem subject only to receivers’ participation constraints. The authors also develop a dual approach to characterize the structure of optimal mechanisms when the good’s characteristics are captured by a one-dimensional variable and all receivers’ utility functions are linear in this variable and reveal an intriguing decoupling structure.

title: The Two Faces of Janus: Dual-Path Moderated Mediation of Observer Responses to Abusive Supervision
The New Rules of Brand Visibility in AI Search
abstract: As LLM-driven search grows, brands are facing two distinct challenges: visibility and accuracy. For AI search, SEO is now entwined with GEO, generative engine optimization. As zero-click LLM responses replace direct links on search result pages, new metrics are replacing traditional traffic analytics. New research suggests ways leaders can ensure that their brands become more visible, more accurately represented, and more competitively positioned over time.

title: New wine, old bottles? Effective strategies of new GenAI firms
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Blending insights from GenAI, strategic reasoning, and empirical grounding in five illustrative ventures, we contribute a theoretical framework for effective strategies of new GenAI firms. They face bifurcated uncertainty (i.e., high uncertainty of a nascent market, moderate uncertainty of a somewhat predictable technology trajectory) such that two complementary strategic logics —Process Perspective (PP) and Resource‐based View (RBV)—are relevant. Second, we identify process‐based (i.e., well‐designed business model and product innovation process) and resource‐based (i.e., superior data, efficient orchestration, complementary resources) advantages. Some relate to GenAI, some generalize. Third, we address what is unique about GenAI entrepreneurship, including strategic implications of GenAI, technology strategy when there is upstream technical dominance and many downstream firms, and a cross‐technology comparison with technologies like software and predictive AI. Managerial Summary The rapid trajectory of GenAI is stunning. Yet many new GenAI firms are simply thin wrappers around well‐known LLMs. Drawing on five illustrative ventures, we contribute a framework for effective strategies for new GenAI firms. These firms face bifurcated uncertainty (i.e., high uncertainty of a nascent market, moderate uncertainty of a somewhat predictable technology trajectory). This calls for creating advantage by navigating high uncertainty markets to accomplish key strategic tasks and relying on foresight to build strategically valuable resources. Specifically, we identify process‐based (well‐designed business model and product innovation process) and resource‐based (i.e., superior data, efficient orchestration, complementary resources) advantages. We also address what is unique about GenAI entrepreneurship, including strategic implications of GenAI and a cross‐technology comparison with technologies like software, predictive AI, and quantum.

title: Whither business model innovation strategy in the age of AI ?
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We argue that business models are transformed into auto‐adaptive systems through embedded AI inference and learning activities. The competitive advantage of focal firms may increasingly depend on how effectively their activity systems learn relative to competing business models, with learning serving as a meta value driver. Such learning‐based advantages may be difficult to replicate when they are costly to create, path dependent, anchored in distinctive accumulated data, and rely on tightly coupled recursive feedback loops among business model activities. Entrepreneurs and corporate leaders thus become architects and curators of evolving learning systems and innovators of novel business models that are critical to their firm's value creation and sustainable performance. Managerial Summary The competitive advantage of focal firms increasingly depends on new AI learning and inference activities, which serve as meta‐value drivers in business models that learn faster, more broadly, and more reliably than competing business models. These dynamic learning‐based advantages are difficult to replicate because they are costly, path dependent, anchored in specific accumulated data, and rely on tightly coupled recursive feedback loops among business model activities. In this paper we argue that entrepreneurs and corporate leaders need to become architects and curators of evolving, auto‐adaptive learning systems and innovators of novel business models that are critical to their firm's value creation and sustainable performance.

title: Toward a (More) Comprehensive CPA Framework: A Reply to “Beyond Statically Motivated, Rational, and Atomistic Actors”
The Effect of Small Quasi-Cash Rewards on Prosocial Behavior: The Case of Voluntary Plasma Donations
abstract: To better understand how prosocial behavior can be effectively encouraged, we study four unresolved issues: whether small rewards also motivate prosocial behavior, how short-term effects differ from longer-run behavioral adjustments, whether incentives induce substitution away from other prosocial activities, and whether reminders about existing rewards meaningfully influence behavior. We examine these issues in a long-run randomized field experiment across 12 donation centers of the Belgian Red Cross-Flanders. Donors normally receive one thank-you-coupon (worth €1.5) for a blood donation and two coupons for a plasma donation. Informing donors about the existing rewards increases plasma donations by 4.6% during the nine-month information period, although this effect fades with repeated reminders. Rewarding plasma donors with an extra coupon raises plasma donations by an additional 7.1% during the six-month reward period; this effect grows during the reward period but disappears immediately afterward. We also document a substitution effect; the plasma reward reduces blood donations by 3.3%. Survey evidence suggests that small rewards act as signals of increased need or as gifts eliciting reciprocity and that our findings may extend to volunteering decisions more broadly. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, Behavioral Economics and Decision Analysis. Funding: This paper is based on research funded by the Belgian Red Cross-Flanders; the content reflects solely the views of the authors and not those of the Red Cross. title: Repricing the green transition: market reactions to COP26 among MNCs diversified in pollution havens
‘Don’t forget to post it on LinkedIn’: Identity regulation and the assetization of employees’ online selves
abstract: What happens to employees’ sense of who they are online when their organization tells them how to present themselves on LinkedIn? Companies increasingly intervene in employees’ professional social media presence through training programs and internal policies, encouraging them to treat their profile as an asset to be cultivated for future return. Drawing on a 2-year digital ethnography of an in-company LinkedIn training program in a French state-owned enterprise, this article shows how the training regulates participants’ sense of their online selves by first denying that their profile has anything to do with who they are, and only then inviting them to reinvest it with personal meaning within the frame this denial has established. Regulation here operates on the identity stakes of the profile itself: on how much of themselves participants take it to carry. The uneven ways participants took up this invitation point to the entanglement of identity regulation and assetization, and to the capacity of an online self, once assetized, to keep generating value for the organization long after the person behind it has disengaged.

title: Intersubjective resilience: Sustaining collective life under persistent life-and-death risk
abstract: How do organizations sustain collective life when exposure to life-and-death risk becomes a persistent condition of work? Based on an ethnographic study of two elite police units operating under continuous life-and-death risk, we find that organizations sustain coordinated collective life not by eliminating fear, resolving contradictions, or restoring stability, but by continually reorganizing these pressures into shared forms of action. We identify three interrelated organizing mechanisms. First, aspirational discipline transforms vulnerability into collective moral obligation by aligning individual striving with shared purpose. Second, paradoxical knotting enables members to act through enduring tensions, such as aggression and restraint or autonomy and obedience, without having to resolve them. Third, routine enactment restores coordinated action through recurring practices of training, reflection, and operational work. Together, these mechanisms explain how organizations maintain coherent and coordinated action when danger is an everyday condition of work. We conceptualize this capacity as intersubjective resilience : the collective accomplishment through which members repeatedly transform fear, contradiction, and disruption into coordinated action under persistent life-and-death risk.

title: The moderating role of tough love on relations between servant leadership and follower outcomes
abstract: Is servant leadership really a Disneyland-inspired fantasy of sunshine, lollipops, and hand-holding that makes followers complacent and lowers the bottom line of organizations, as critics claim? This criticism overlooks that servant leaders, striving to bring out the full potential in followers, do not only give positive strokes but may also provide followers with critical feedback. To assess the role of critical feedback in mitigating the flaws of servant leadership raised by critics, this study introduces tough love, the delivery of criticism with a positive tone and clear intent to help recipients overcome their deficiencies. We hypothesize that the relationship between servant leadership and key outcomes, such as follower performance, is strengthened the more servant leaders provide followers with tough love. We contend that tough love is appreciated by followers, solidifies relationships with their leaders, and helps them to grow through self-expansion. We reason that this growth benefits their work behaviors and attitudes. With multi-source field data covering three points in time, controlling for positive and negative feedback and prior levels of dependent variables, tough love is shown to moderate relations between servant leadership and both in-role performance and organizational citizenship behaviors, with mixed results for creativity and turnover intentions.

title: From Data to Decisions: Marketing Analytics, Mental Performance, and Firm Growth in an Emerging Market
abstract: Using a field experiment with 550 Rwandan firms, we show marketing analytics causally enhances entrepreneurs’ cognition and raises firm sales and profits.

title: Can Facebook Ads Prevent Malaria? Two Field Experiments in India
abstract: Two field experiments evaluate a nationwide Facebook malaria prevention campaign in India, finding effects concentrated in urban, more advantaged populations.

title: Exploitation in the marketplace: A consumer behavior perspective
abstract: Abstract This paper examines exploitation in the marketplace from a consumer behavior perspective. We define marketplace exploitation as occurring when one party leverages structural and/or situational resource asymmetries to extract disproportionate value in ways that undermine fairness or autonomy, even when exchanges appear voluntary and mutually beneficial. We distinguish marketplace exploitation from related concepts including fairness, deception, and discrimination, arguing that it centers on the morally problematic use of contextual advantage. Adopting a dual lens, we develop conceptual frameworks for both firm‐to‐consumer exploitation (e.g., price gouging, dark patterns) and consumer‐to‐firm exploitation (e.g., free trial abuse, exploiting firm mistakes). These frameworks delineate how structural and situational asymmetries give rise to objective exploitative acts, when such acts are perceived as exploitative, and how they shape emotional, cognitive, and behavioral responses. We synthesize a research agenda and outline methodological approaches for studying the antecedents, perceptions, and consequences of exploitation. This work contributes to consumer psychology by conceptualizing marketplace exploitation as both a subjective psychological experience and a strategic marketplace behavior, with implications for theory, policy, and ethical firm practices.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

title: Heterogeneous beliefs, asset prices, and business cycles
abstract: We develop a complete-market production economy in which heterogeneous beliefs about productivity growth affect both asset prices and real activity. Firms must hire workers before productivity is realized, so operating leverage increases the exposure of profits to productivity risk. Because the firm’s discount factor depends on a wealth-weighted aggregation of investor beliefs, shifts in optimism compress risk premia and raise employment, while reversals trigger contractions. This mechanism generates an equilibrium feedback between asset prices, hiring, and risk exposure. A taxonomy of belief systems shows that only extrapolative beliefs produce amplification and endogenous risk build-up. Disciplined by survey expectations, the model jointly matches key asset-pricing, trading-volume, and business-cycle moments.

title: Convexity of Inverse Blocking Curves in Loss Systems
abstract: Why Larger Service Systems Benefit More from Scale How much extra demand can a service system handle when capacity is increased while keeping the same target level of customer blocking? In the paper “Convexity of Inverse Blocking Curves in Loss Systems,” Benjamin Legros establishes an exact economies-of-scale result for loss systems. The paper proves that the maximum supportable demand is an increasing and globally convex function of the number of servers. In practical terms, as a system becomes larger, each additional server can support progressively more additional demand while maintaining the same blocking target. Equivalently, the extra capacity required to accommodate additional demand decreases as the system grows. The result provides a rigorous mathematical foundation for resource pooling in capacity-constrained services. It applies to the classical Erlang-B loss model and extends to systems with a finite waiting room, with potential relevance for telecommunications, healthcare, emergency response, and other service operations.
